source.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Antibody Language Models Using SAEs
source.authors: Rebonto Haque; Oliver M. Turnbull; Anisha Parsan; Nithin Parsan; John J. Yang; Anna L. Beukenhorst; Charlotte M. Deane

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplement are present. There are minor PDF extraction and equation-formatting artifacts.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether SAE-derived features in antibody language models are predictive and steerable, and reports that predictive TopK features do not reliably control generation while Ordered SAE features can. This refines claims about dictionary features as model units, but it does not test toy-model superposition.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses superposition and polysemantic neurons as background, but does not test feature count versus dimension, sparsity-dependent transitions, importance-dependent geometry, or whether extra features are dropped. The recorded results are its own SAE probing, activation-pattern, and steering results; cited findings from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study trains TopK and Ordered SAEs on three antibody language models. It reports whether single latents recover antibody concepts beyond a prevalence baseline and beyond neurons (V4), and whether those latents causally steer generation (V5). This is a new domain, autoregressive protein/antibody LMs, not general-purpose LLMs, so T3. The TopK steering failure is also a specific argument that predictive dictionary features are not necessarily the model's causal units. No toy-model, capacity, or dimensionality test is run.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors conclude that TopK SAEs recover biologically meaningful antibody features, but high feature–concept correlation does not guarantee causal steering. Ordered SAEs reliably expose steerable features across three antibody LMs, at the cost of less interpretable activation patterns. They recommend TopK for concept mapping and Ordered SAEs for steering.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains TopK and Ordered SAEs on antibody-language-model activations and probes or steers antibody concepts; it does not implement or reproduce the toy-network superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature recovery varies by gene identity, layer, and model architecture; the paper reports no strong TopK features for some gene/model combinations. TopK versus Ordered SAE choice changes steering success and activation interpretability.
record.problems: The authors describe steering analyses as not exhaustive and acknowledge that annotated antibody data are limited. Several activation-pattern results are qualitative, and exact steering proportions are shown in figures rather than stated numerically. TopK feature counts depend on an acknowledged somewhat arbitrary F1 threshold.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported results were left out.

untested.parts: No toy networks, feature/dimension sweeps, sparsity transition or geometry.
No test of capacity competition or importance-based allocation.
Neuron polysemanticity is mentioned as a possible explanation only. No test of its cause.
Only antibody LMs (13M–764M), not general-purpose LLMs. No measure of how features spread across neurons beyond a qualitative CDRH3 comparison.
Completeness and stability across seeds or training runs are not tested. Cross-model feature consistency is discussed but not measured.
No test of one- vs multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: Authors tried steering TopK features across all p-IgGen layers and multiple genes and could not steer predictably (data not shown). This broadens the V5 TopK failure beyond IGHJ4 at layer 3.

Top IGHJ4-predictive TopK latents (463, 4720) fire at IMGT 119/120, which are residues conserved across all IGHJ genes. Only 6276 fires on the IGHJ4-specific Y117, so predictive features do not match the concept.
IgLM and ProGen2-OAS TopK IGHJ features show weaker positional consistency than p-IgGen. The authors attribute this to low TopK feature consistency across architectures (qualitative only).

record.verdict_notes: The domain is antibody/protein LMs, not general LLMs, so V4 and V5 verdicts hold only in that setting. R1–R8 are whole-dictionary probes and cannot show sparse single-feature recovery. R12 and R16 are the same result. The feature threshold is acknowledged as somewhat arbitrary. TopK and Ordered SAEs differ in expansion factor (32x vs 8x) and training data size (full vs 100k sequences), which confounds the architecture comparison. Steering analyses are not exhaustive. Supplementary A.1 mentions Matryoshka-like nesting limiting feature splitting only as a hypothesis.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-network feature/dimension sweep, sparsity-dependent transition, or regular-geometry test.
No test of capacity competition, dedicated dimensions for important features, or sharing of less important features.
No test of polysemantic neurons arising without capacity pressure.
Tests SAE recovery of antibody-related concepts in antibody language models, not feature spreading across neurons or dictionary recovery in general-purpose LLMs.
Does not establish SAE feature completeness or stability across training runs; tests concept prediction, activation patterns, and steering.
No test of whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional subspaces.

relationships.condition: p-IgGen layers 0–3 and IgLM/ProGen2-OAS final layers, for genes where single TopK latents pass the feature criterion
relationships.reason: Single latents predict IGHJ identity above a prevalence+0.2 threshold (R9–R11, R14, R15, R18). Other models show high-scoring features (R19, R21–R25). A latent localizes to CDRH3 where neurons scatter (R30, R31).
relationships.display_finding: Single latents predicted IGHJ identity above a prevalence-plus-0.2 threshold, other models also showed high-scoring features, and one latent localized to CDRH3 where neurons scattered.

source_check.reason: The cited results show recoverable antibody concepts and localized latent activations. The criterion is F1 > 2π/(1+π)+0.2, not prevalence+0.2; numerical cutoffs for IgLM and ProGen2-OAS are not reported.

relationships.condition: Specific genes and models: p-IgGen IGHJ5; IgLM and ProGen2-OAS IGHJ2 and IGHJ5; weak cases
relationships.reason: No qualifying feature for IGHJ5 in p-IgGen (R17) or for IGHJ2/IGHJ5 in the other models (R26–R29). Several passes are marginal (R12, R13, R16, R20), so recovery depends on concept and model.
relationships.display_finding: No qualifying feature was found for IGHJ5 in p-IgGen, or for IGHJ2 and IGHJ5 in IgLM and ProGen2-OAS. Several passes were marginal, so recovery depends on the concept and model.

relationships.condition: p-IgGen TopK SAE latents predictive of IGHJ4, layer 3
relationships.reason: Positive steering on the three top predictive TopK latents produced no predictable change in IGHJ4 usage (R32–R34). Top latents mark residues conserved across genes, so predictive features are not causal units.
relationships.display_finding: Positive steering on the three most predictive TopK latents produced no predictable change in IGHJ4 usage. The top latents mark residues conserved across genes, so being predictive did not make them causal handles.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.condition: p-IgGen TopK SAE latents predictive of IGHJ4, layer 3
source_check.reason: R32–R34 test predictable gene-usage steering, not completeness, stability or canonicity in V5. Only one tested latent passes the feature criterion; two mark conserved residues, while latent 6276 marks an IGHJ4-specific residue. Failure to steer does not establish that these are not representational units.

relationships.condition: Ordered SAE latents in p-IgGen, IgLM and ProGen2-OAS versus TopK latents
relationships.reason: Ordered latents steer strongly (r=0.94, −0.98, 0.87, 0.99; R35–R38) while TopK latents do not (R32–R34). Whether dictionary features act as causal units depends on the SAE architecture chosen.
relationships.display_finding: Ordered latents steered strongly (r = 0.94, −0.98, 0.87, 0.99) while TopK latents did not, so whether features act as causal units depended on the SAE architecture.
